Great Expectations or other Data Quality frameworks.

The biggest risk for a small company in the AI race is the person at the top.

Transforming a business with AI is a business decision before it is a technology decision. So an SME's chances depend on who inside it understands both the business and the technology. I rank those chances in four levels.

1. The CEO has personally rebuilt at least one part of how the company works, hands-on, with AI. Buying a tool does not count. Nobody has to convince the person who signs the budget, so decisions take days instead of quarters.

2. One manager has the mandate and the budget to change how work is done with AI, and has already used it at least once. This person knows both the technology and the business. From the inside, they can push a decision through faster than any outside consultant, and they can check every constraint themselves, on the shop floor and with the people who live with it.

3. The company hires outside help. Consultants bring method and an outside view, but they rarely know your business as well as your own people. A consultant without an insider champion is a rental. When the contract ends, the knowledge leaves with them.

4. The company waits. It treats AI as a step for later and assumes it can join when the picture is clearer. By then the first competitor in its niche will have redesigned its operations around AI. If the business is digital and scalable, that competitor can turn the advantage into market share faster than the others can react. In a physical business it takes longer, but the gap still grows every month.

The consultants worth hiring make the person inside who decides stronger. This is the principle behind a new offering we are building at PCG - Public Cloud Group: one sponsor inside the client, a roadmap that lives in the client's own systems and no clients who want us to decide for them.

I describe the extreme on purpose. There are steps between these levels and every company needs them. But if your company sits at level 3 or 4, the first step is to find the person who will own AI in your company. If there is nobody, that person is you.

B2B brands are boring.
They have no personality.

Or at least, that's what you'd think looking at most of them.

Same shade of blue. Stock photography or, worse, AI graphics. Buzzwords (ew).

Same websites that could belong to any company.

I think that's a problem.

Because behind every business decision, whether it's choosing your software, hiring your agency or signing a contract, there's still a human.

They have preferences. They remember brands that make an impression.

So how do you make your brand memorable?

1. Do a branding exercise
Decide what you want your clients to remember your brand for.
Is it irony? Boldness? Friendliness? Warmth?

Look at Intuit Mailchimp. Mailchimp has built its identity around creativity, approachability and a quirky personality. Its illustrations, copy and visual identity all reinforce that.

2. Pick three adjectives and stick to them
It's okay to adapt your tone of voice depending on the medium of communication, but don't change your brand's personality when you switch from social media to email.

Like Slack. Slack has a friendly, human and accessible personality. Its product, website and communications feel like they come from the same brand.

3. Don't be afraid to push boundaries
Nothing memorable comes from always sticking to your comfort zone. So don't be afraid to push the boundaries a little.

Gong is the perfect example. They use bold messaging, distinctive visuals and a confident tone in a category that can easily feel technical and corporate.

The bench isn’t a failure. It’s an active business phase.

When a permanent employee is between projects, they usually get a chance to grab a coffee, clear their inbox and catch a breath. 

When an IT contractor is between contracts, the business doesn’t pause. You start working ON your business (rather than working IN your business):

• Advertising and Marketing Department: You stop waiting for recruiters to come to you. You proactively message hiring managers, rewrite your CV, follow up with past clients, reach out to your warm network, and set daily targets for outreach. Visibility is a full-time job when you’re not billing.

• HR and Training Manager: You use the quiet period to close skill gaps that directly affect day rate and become a certification machine. Cloud, security, AI, architecture, or the specific platform your next client is asking for. The contractors who land the premium rates after a quiet spell are usually the ones who turned downtime into demonstrable progress.

• Business Development: You comment, post insights, update your profile with recent outcomes, turn on your "open to work" banner, and stay on top of your LinkedIn networking. Most good contracts still come through people who already know (or have recently seen) your name.

• CFO: You review the war chest. How many months of runway do you actually have? Are your tax reserves solid? Are there any Companies House or tax deadlines that are imminent? The contractors who stay calm in a slow market are the ones who already know their numbers.

Contracting is cyclical. Quiet periods happen. Feast and famine are real. The difference is whether you treat the bench as dead-time or as a deliberate investment phase.

What is a Global Capability Centre (GCC), and why do so many global companies build one in India?

We turned the answer into a 75-second rhyme. Here's the story behind it.

A GCC is a company's own team working out of India. It isn't a vendor or an outsourcing contract. The people carry the same badge, report to the same leaders and chase the same targets as headquarters.

How it started, and where it stands today:
- 1985: Texas Instruments opens an R&D centre in Bangalore, the first multinational to do so in India
- 2,117 GCCs as of March 2026, employing about 2.36 million people (Nasscom-Zinnov India GCC Landscape 2026)
- More than two new GCCs open in India every week
- 250+ of them now focus on AI
- Wells Fargo and GE run large centres in Hyderabad, and GCC teams work from Pune, Chennai, Delhi NCR, Bengaluru and beyond

Why India?
Talent comes first. In HFS Research's 2026 study, 40% of companies named talent as their main reason for building a GCC in India. The second reason is control. Deloitte points to IP and data protection as a big part of why companies choose their own centre over outsourcing. When the team is yours, so are the code and the data.

The hard part is the setup: hiring, payroll, office space and compliance. GCCNexus handles all four, so your India team is up and running in weeks, not months.

Nearly 75% of organisations plan to adopt agentic AI. Only 21% have a mature governance framework.

That gap is the real story of 2026.

Agents have quietly moved from demos into execution: finance close, procurement, customer operations, hiring. The models are good enough. The operating model usually isn't.

Before your next agent goes live, answer three questions.

1. Who owns it?
Not "IT". A named human with a stake in the outcome and the authority to switch it off.

2. What can't it touch?
Define the no-go zone (payments, contracts, personal data, anything irreversible) before day one, not after the first incident.

3. What does success look like in numbers?
An agent without a baseline is expensive enthusiasm. Cycle time, error rate, cost per case. Pick one and track it weekly.

The organisations pulling ahead are not the ones with the most agents. They redesigned the work first, then let agents slot into it. And they are honest about the human side: fewer people doing routine handling, more people supervising, designing and improving the system.

Don't automate a broken process. You will just produce broken outcomes faster.

Working at maybe the most crazy production studio in the country, if not the world, can't be easy.

Klik Klak gave us "Kazhetsya, nashchupal", Little Big and "Zashkvarnye istorii". Almost 7 million subscribers and 1.5 billion views on YouTube.

Behind the camera, there's more emotion, drama and intrigue than in any IT company. So when the founders asked me to help build a culture, keep the business standing and stop the team from running away, I said yes.

I started by listening: a survey of 18 employees and 11 one-on-one interviews.

One answer stuck with me: "Approvals take several weeks. Nobody knows who makes the final call." Because gifted and talent teams usually focus on creative processes not even clear result.

The team's top three asks:
• clear briefs
• one person who makes the final decision
• less toxicity between teams

What I designed:
• a RACI matrix for key production stages, agreed before every project
• an org structure with teams and leads, plus roles worth hiring permanently
• KPIs in contracts: numbers for sales and marketing, A/B/C ratings for creatives
• hiring: video editors, marketers and an AI video creator with a 200k+ audience

One thing I advised against: a showrunner. That's one more decision-maker in a chain that already had too many.

My takeaway: even in the wildest creative team, conflict is often not about people. It's about roles nobody wrote down.

———

Работать в самом трешовом продакшене страны, а то и мира, не может быть просто.

Клик Клак подарил нам «Кажется, нащупал», Little Big и «Зашкварные истории». На YouTube — почти 7 млн подписчиков и 1,5 млрд просмотров.

За кадром столько эмоций, интриг и драмы, что любая айтишка прикурит. Поэтому, когда основатели попросили помочь выстроить культуру, чтобы бизнес не рухнул, а команда не разбежалась, я согласилась.

Начала с того, что слушала: опрос 18 сотрудников и 11 интервью один на один.

Один ответ я запомнила: «Согласования занимают несколько недель. Никто не понимает, кто принимает финальное решение».

Три главные просьбы команды:
• понятная постановка задач
• один человек, который принимает финальное решение
• меньше токсичности между «цехами»

Что я разработала:
• RACI-матрицу для ключевых этапов продакшна — утверждать до старта проекта
• оргструктуру с отделами и тимлидами плюс роли, которые стоит взять в штат
• KPI в договорах: цифры для продаж и маркетинга, оценки A/B/C для креативщиков
• найм: монтажёров, маркетологов и AI-видеокреатора с аудиторией 200 тыс.+

От одного я отговорила: вводить шоураннера. Это ещё один голос в цепочке, где решающих и так слишком много.

Мой вывод: даже в самой безумной творческой команде конфликты часто не про людей. Они про роли, которые никто не записал.

One missing sentence is keeping you trapped in routine approvals.

Every approval request lands in your inbox because nobody ever wrote down when the previous answer was "yes"

There are 9 types of approvals I keep seeing in businesses and all it takes to hand them off is a single sentence for each.

Write one line for each of the 9, then test it on the next real request that comes in

1. Discounts: approve it if the client pays on time and the discount matches one you've given before, escalate anything new

2. Refunds: approve it when the work clearly missed what the client signed, escalate when the client is disputing what was agreed

3. Supplier choices: approve it when the supplier is already on the approved list, escalate when it's a first order with someone new

4. Scope changes: approve it when the extra work fits inside the current deadline, escalate when it moves the delivery date

5. Overtime: approve it when a client deadline would otherwise be missed, escalate when it's the third week in a row

6. Software renewals: approve it when the tool was used every week last quarter, escalate when nobody can name who uses it

7. Deadline extensions: approve it when the client asks before the original date, escalate when the delay has already happened

8. Hiring a freelancer: approve it for a role you've filled the same way before, escalate for any new type of work

9. Payment terms: approve it when the client asks for the terms in your standard contract, escalate any request to change them

Each rule gets tested the first time someone uses it, and the gaps show up in the requests that still reach you

I work through this with owners because every rule written is one less message waiting for you on a Friday

Pick the decision that reached you most often and write its line today

The gap between a 12 LPA and a 40 LPA SDET is not more tools. It's this JD

Most SDETs read a Senior job post as a longer list of tools.
It isn't. It's a different job.

I took a real one. Veeam. Senior SDET, Bangalore, 8+ years.
Then I mapped every line to what the job actually tests.

Here is what each line means, and where most "senior" candidates go quiet.

1) "Design, build and scale automation frameworks"
↳ Can 300 tests still run clean after 6 months.
Most people have only written tests inside a framework someone else built. They never made the design calls themselves.

2) "Write clean, high quality automation code"
↳ Is your test code reviewed like product code.
Hardcoded data, copy-pasted locators, raw waits. That is tutorial code, not senior code.

3) "Build internal tools, mock services and data utilities"
↳ Can you unblock testing when the API isn't ready yet.
A lot of SDETs only consume test data. They have never built a mock or a data factory.

4) "Integrate suites into CI (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab)"
↳ Do your tests run headless, in parallel, and pass the same way every time.
"Works on my machine" is where most frameworks quietly die.

5) "Test plans across functional, integration, regression, performance"
↳ Can you decide what NOT to automate.
A senior knows what to skip. Automating everything usually means there is no risk model.

6) "Partner with PMs and engineers in the design phase"
↳ Can you catch the bug in the design review, before the code exists.
Most testers enter after the build is done and test what already shipped.

7) "Test REST and GraphQL APIs"
↳ Contract level checks, not status code checks.
The dangerous API bug isn't a 500. It's a 200 with the wrong body.

Read it again.
Every gap is the same gap.
You can write tests. You have never designed the system that runs them.
That is the line between an SDET and a Senior SDET.

Imagine hiring an IT services company to complete a software project.
Traditionally, the proposal might involve a team of developers, testers and project managers working over several months.
The price would reflect the people and time required.
Now imagine that AI tools allow the same team to complete parts of the project much faster.
That's good news for the customer.
But it creates an awkward question for the service provider.
Should the customer pay less because fewer working hours are needed?
Or should the provider earn more because it delivers the same result with greater efficiency?
This tension sits behind some of the concerns surrounding traditional IT services companies.
Several major Indian technology brands have experienced sharp declines in estimated brand value, with AI disruption affecting expectations for their business models.
The challenge is particularly significant for companies accustomed to measuring projects through staffing and utilization.
AI increases the importance of discussing outcomes.
A client commissioning a system doesn't necessarily care how many hours were spent writing the code.
They care whether it works reliably, solves the intended problem and remains maintainable.
Of course, outcome-based contracts introduce risks.
A service provider needs to estimate complexity carefully and agree on what successful delivery actually means.
Unexpected requirements can make a fixed commitment expensive.
Still, the direction of the market seems clear.
As technology makes work faster, pricing models built mainly around the quantity of labor will face increasing scrutiny.

One observation in the recent discussion about Indian IT brands stood out to me.
Research and development shouldn't become a priority only when a company's existing business starts facing pressure.
That sounds simple, but it can be difficult for established service companies.
When a business has reliable customers and a profitable operating model, there are strong incentives to keep improving what already works.
Hiring more people, expanding delivery centers and winning larger contracts can appear more predictable than investing in uncertain research.
The problem is that technological change rarely waits for a convenient moment.
By the time a new technology starts affecting revenue, competitors may already have years of experience developing products around it.
AI is creating exactly this kind of challenge.
Companies that mainly adopted existing software tools may find themselves competing against businesses that have invested deeply in automation, data platforms and proprietary technology.
Those investments take time to mature.
Researchers need opportunities to experiment.
Early products may not generate meaningful revenue.
Some projects will fail.
A company focused entirely on short-term financial performance may struggle to justify that uncertainty.
But avoiding it can create a larger problem later.
I think established IT firms need a more deliberate balance between serving existing customers and building capabilities for future markets.
The strongest research programs don't necessarily produce immediate headlines.
Their value often becomes visible when the rest of the industry suddenly needs something the company has been developing for years.

Yesterday I wrote that India is being bought as a hedge against the AI trade, and that the capital is concentrating. Part 1 ended with a promise: the real value is going somewhere most boards are not looking.

Here is the payoff. Three places, all visible this week.

1️⃣ The application layer, not the model layer.

Of the $114 million that went into Indian AI startups this week, the biggest cheque was $53 million to Dreamteam, an application-layer B2B company. Physical AI startup Humyn Labs raised $47 million — $26 million in equity led by Accel plus $21 million in venture debt. Disseqt AI raised $8 million for AI governance. The market is paying for deployment, data and control, not for another model.

2️⃣ Sovereign capability has become a procurement argument.

At Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, Sarvam AI's Vivek Raghavan made the case for Sarvam-105B — a 105-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model trained from scratch in India on IndiaAI Mission compute, built for 22 Indian languages and voice-first use. The question it forces on every CTO is blunt: do we own our AI, or do we keep renting it?

3️⃣ Talent is the real bottleneck, and the numbers are uncomfortable.

90% of Indian employers are expanding tech teams, yet 63% expect net reductions in tech headcount within 12-24 months, and 44% are hiring fewer entry-level developers than two years ago. AI-qualified developers command more than twice entry-level pay. 72% of employers say running AI tools costs as much as, or more than, junior talent for comparable work. Contract staffing in Indian IT grew 10.1% in FY26, against 2.3% for permanent roles.

4️⃣ And the exit problem nobody wants to name.

India has over 4,500 deep-tech startups and funding is flowing, yet the exit landscape stays thin. The bottleneck is not innovation. It is that too few Indian companies are buyers of deep tech.

✅ Do fund the unglamorous middle — data, integration, governance, change management.

✅ Do move a slice of your AI budget into reskilling the team you already have. It is cheaper than the market rate.

❌ Don't buy an AI narrative you cannot operate.

❌ Don't wait for a clearer picture. The picture is being drawn by whoever deploys first.

The leadership test of this decade is not who has the best model. It is who converts a $1.8 trillion global buildout into Indian productivity, Indian jobs and Indian margins — and who stays content renting someone else's.

Capital is rotating. Capability is not. Build the second one.
